title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Network monitor for macOS · free and open source See every connection your Mac makes. Switchboard draws a live picture of the network on your Mac: which program is talking, to whom, how much, and for how long. It has six ways to look at it, a filter language, a timeline you can drag back, and a log you can search. It watches and never blocks, and it sends nothing anywhere. curl -fsSL https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/switchboard/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash Paste it into Terminal. Version 0.1.1, a beta, for Macs with Apple silicon on macOS 15 or later. The installer checks the download against the release's checksum and asks before anything that needs your password. Install R

title: Overview
heading: Six ways to look at the same traffic
text: Press 1 to 6 to switch. Whatever you have selected stays selected, so you can follow one program from one picture to the next. The layouts → 1Constellation The whole machine at a glance. 2Flow Where the bytes go: program, then protocol, then whoever owns the far end. 3Lanes What happened when: a row per program, a bar per connection. 4Globe Where in the world your traffic goes. 5Hierarchy Account, program, domain, and address, as a tree. 6Cyberspace The address space as a floor in 3D, to fly through. Full mode

title: Overview
heading: Names, not just numbers
text: On its own, Switchboard needs no password and sees every connection your account makes. Add its small collector, which runs as root, and it sees every account's connections and reads hostnames from DNS answers and TLS handshakes. The Health tab installs it, and removes it again. Standalone and Full → Cyberspace

title: Overview
heading: The internet as a place you can learn
text: Addresses run along a Hilbert curve, so every block of addresses is a block of floor and the same address is always in the same place. Cloud providers become districts you recognise. Each destination is a tower as tall as the bytes it has carried and as bright as its rate. Drag to orbit, and fly with W A S D. Flying through it → History

title: Overview
heading: Drag back in time
text: The timeline replays the last fifteen minutes in the graph, or up to an hour. Older traffic is in a SQLite log on your Mac that you search with the same filter, replay in the graph, and export as CSV or JSON lines. The log → Filtering

title: Overview
heading: One filter for everything
text: The same language narrows the graph, the tables, and the log. Values understand units, wildcards, and networks, and terms combine with AND, OR, NOT, and brackets. The filter language → process:Slack rate_out>100KB/s user:root service:SSH r_port:443 NOT host:*.apple.com age>1h bytes<10KB class:public country!=US signing=unsigned remote:10.0.0.0/8 OR tag:office On a wall

title: Overview
heading: Made to be watched
text: Kiosk mode shows nothing but the graph and keeps the display awake. Six colour themes include one whose hues stay distinct with the common colour-vision deficiencies. A saved workspace starts a wall display in one command. Workspaces and walls →

title: Overview
heading: What it does not do
text: It never blocks, changes, or injects anything. It watches, and that is all. It sends nothing anywhere. No telemetry, no update checks, no crash reports. It keeps no packet contents. Only who talked to whom, how much, and when. It goes online only when you ask: to download the free location databases, and for reverse DNS lookups if you turn them on. Privacy →

title: Installing
heading: Installing
text: Installing Switchboard needs a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later) and macOS 15 or later. It has only been tested on macOS 27.

title: Installing
heading: With the installer (recommended)
text: curl -fsSL https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/switchboard/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash The installer: checks this is an Apple silicon Mac on macOS 15 or later; downloads the release's zip and checks it against the SHA-256 written into the installer, so it installs nothing that differs from what was released; puts Switchboard.app in /Applications, quitting and replacing a copy already there; asks whether to install the collector (Full mode), with sudo, which asks for your password; a collector already installed is updated without asking, so it matches the app; asks whether to download the location databases, unless you have them; opens Switchboard. Run it again to update. To re

title: Installing
heading: From the zip
text: Download Switchboard-<version>-arm64.zip from the releases page, open it, and drag Switchboard.app to Applications. Switchboard is signed ad hoc, not with a Developer ID, and is not notarised, so the first time you open it macOS says it cannot check it. Open System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security, scroll to Security, and click Open Anyway; you are asked once. To check the zip first, compare shasum -a 256 Switchboard-<version>-arm64.zip with the release's SHA256SUMS. Everything else is in the app: the Health tab installs the collector and Settings ▸ Location downloads the location data.

title: Installing
heading: From source
text: You need Xcode or its command line tools, with Swift 6. git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/switchboard.git cd switchboard && scripts/bundle.sh open build/Switchboard.app Nothing is downloaded during the build; Switchboard has no third-party dependencies. scripts/release.sh tests and builds a release in build/release: the zip, install.sh with the zip's checksum filled in, and SHA256SUMS. With --publish it creates the GitHub release from them, from a clean main that has been pushed.

title: Installing
heading: What goes where
text: What Where The app, with the collector, sbctl, and the scripts it runs inside it /Applications/Switchboard.app The collector, once installed /usr/local/libexec/switchboardd, started by /Library/LaunchDaemons/io.github.robert-mcdermott.switchboard.collector.plist, logging to /var/log/switchboardd.log The log and the location databases ~/Library/Application Support/Switchboard Settings and workspaces The app's preferences, io.github.robert-mcdermott.switchboard.app Builds before 0.1.0 used the identifier local.switchboard. The first launch of 0.1.0 carries their settings over, and installing the collector replaces the old one.

title: Standalone and Full
heading: Standalone and Full
text: Standalone and Full Switchboard runs in one of two modes, shown at the top left of the window. Standalone needs nothing installed and no password. It sees the connections of the account you are logged in as. What it cannot see: Connections made by other accounts and by system daemons running as root (for example mDNSResponder, syspolicyd, software-update and security agents). Hostnames. Without packet capture there are no DNS answers or TLS handshakes to read names from, so destinations show as addresses unless you turn on active lookups (Troubleshooting says how). A small share of your own sockets, about 5 to 8%, which the system's statistics interface does not report to an unprivileged pro

title: The window
heading: Layouts
text: Key Layout Good for 1 Constellation The whole machine at a glance 2 Flow Where the bytes go: process, then protocol, then whoever owns the far end 3 Lanes What happened when: one row per process, a bar per connection 4 Globe Where in the world your traffic goes 5 Hierarchy Account, process, domain, address, as a tree 6 Cyberspace The address space as a floor, in 3D, to fly through Whatever you select stays selected when you switch.

title: The window
heading: Cyberspace
text: The floor is the address space. IPv4 is the square on the left and IPv6's global addresses (2000::/3) the one on the right. Addresses run along a Hilbert curve, which keeps neighbouring addresses together, so each block of addresses is a block of floor. The grid divides each square into 16 × 16 blocks: an IPv4 /8 apiece, labelled where something stands in it (52/8), or an IPv6 /11 (2600::/11). Link-local and unique-local IPv6 addresses stand in the gap between the squares, under this Mac. A tower stands on each destination's address. Height is the bytes it has carried, brightness its current rate, colour the kind of traffic, and pulses climb it as fast as the traffic goes. A bright ring at t

title: The window
heading: Reading the graph
text: Line thickness and pulses: how much traffic, and which way most of it is going. Colour: what the traffic is. Teal is TLS, violet QUIC, green DNS, amber remote access, orange cleartext. A red ring on a process: unsigned, or its signature does not check out. An amber ring: signed by nobody in particular (normal for things you built or installed with Homebrew), or listening where other machines can reach it. The tooltip says which. A bright ring on a destination: this Mac has never talked to it before, according to the log. Scroll or pinch to zoom. Zooming in spreads things apart much faster than it enlarges them, the way markers on a map stay small: at ten times the zoom, distances are ten tim

title: The window
heading: Profiles
text: Cinema draws at up to 120 frames a second with full glow; for walls and demonstrations. Operator draws at 60 with less glow and more labels, at about half the CPU; for leaving open all day. Still has no motion at all. P cycles between them.

title: The window
heading: Themes
text: T cycles through six colour themes, and Settings ▸ Display ▸ Theme picks one. The choice is kept, and travels with exported settings. Theme Looks like Standard Cyan, violet, and green on deep navy Neon Magenta and cyan on deep violet Phosphor A green phosphor terminal Amber An amber terminal Ice Pale blues and whites on blue-black; the quietest Colour-safe Hues that stay distinct with the common colour-vision deficiencies Every theme keeps a colour of its own for each kind of traffic, a red ring for a program whose signature fails, and warm colours for remote access and cleartext. All are dark: the graph adds light to its background, as a radar screen does. The panels and controls stay as th

title: Filtering
heading: Filtering
text: Filtering The filter field narrows the graph, the tables, and the log search at once. process:Slack rate_out>100KB/s user:root service:SSH r_port:443 NOT host:*.apple.com age>1h bytes<10KB class:public country!=US signing=unsigned remote:10.0.0.0/8 OR tag:office field:value means contains, = and != mean equals, and <, > compare numbers. Values take units (KB/s, MB, h), * wildcards, and networks in CIDR form. Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT, and brackets. A bare word matches process, hostname, service, and address. The ? beside the field lists every field. Note that a destination with no known country matches country!=US. Write class:public country!=US to leave out private addresses.

title: Filtering
heading: Traffic within this Mac
text: Many connections never leave the machine: containers, development servers, databases, and editors talking to each other over loopback or this Mac's own address. On a developer's Mac they can be most of what there is. The laptop button in the top bar, or L, switches them: On (the default): everything, including traffic within this Mac. Off: only traffic to and from other machines. The graph, the tables, and the log search all leave the rest out, and a line at the top left says so. This only changes what is shown. Whether these connections are written to the log at all is a separate setting, in The log.

title: The log
heading: The log
text: The log Every connection is written to a SQLite file at ~/Library/Application Support/Switchboard/log.sqlite. The Log panel searches it with the same filter; drag its slider to show a past moment in the graph. Settings ▸ Log sets how much detail is kept and for how long; the Log panel can erase it. Leave out connections within this Mac stops them being written to the log at all, which keeps it much smaller on a developer's Mac (development tools and containers can open hundreds a minute). They still show live. It is off by default; to hide them from view instead, use the laptop button (L). From the command line: sbctl log query "process:Safari bytes>1MB" --since 7d

title: Location data
heading: Location data
text: Location and network owner Country, city, and network owner come from the free DB-IP Lite databases, about 130 MB. Switchboard downloads them only when you ask: press Download Location Data in Settings ▸ Location, or answer yes when the installer asks. The app uses them as soon as they arrive. DB-IP publishes new ones a day or two into each month; press Download Again whenever you like. From a clone, scripts/fetch-geoip.sh does the same, and the app reads the files at its next start. Check one address with sbctl geo 8.8.8.8. The data is IP Geolocation by DB-IP, licensed CC BY 4.0. The globe also needs to know where this Mac is. It guesses from the time zone; to set it exactly, open Settings

title: Workspaces and walls
heading: Workspaces and walls
text: Workspaces and wall displays The Workspace menu holds named arrangements of layout, profile, filter, and panels. Three come with Switchboard: NOC Wall: the constellation in Cinema, full screen, nothing else. Privacy Audit: the flow layout, public destinations only, the First Seen panel open, ended connections kept. Developer: the constellation in Operator with the connections table. Choose Save Current as Workspace… to add your own. Export Settings… and Import Settings… in the same menu carry workspaces and settings to another Mac as one JSON file. Kiosk mode (K, or ⌃⌘K; Esc leaves) goes full screen, hides everything but the graph and the pointer, and keeps the display awake. To start a wall

title: Troubleshooting
heading: Troubleshooting
text: Troubleshooting The installer says the download does not match the release's checksum. The 0.1.0 installer said this whenever the check could not run, not only when the download was wrong. Two things stopped it running: an Intel-only shasum left in /usr/local/bin by an old Homebrew, which cannot run on a Mac without Rosetta, and Perl settings such as PERL5LIB, which can break macOS's own shasum. Run the install command again to get the current installer, which uses only macOS's own tools. If it still finds a difference, it shows what arrived instead. A few kilobytes of HTML means a proxy or web filter on your network replaced the download: try another network, or install from the zip. It say

title: Privacy
heading: Privacy
text: Privacy Switchboard sends nothing anywhere: no telemetry, no crash reports, no update checks. The one exception is active hostname lookups, which are off unless you choose them. Switchboard ▸ About Switchboard: What It Collects lists exactly what is read, kept, and where.

title: Command line
heading: Command line
text: The command line tool sbctl reads the same engine without the window, and is how most of Switchboard is tested. It travels inside the app: /Applications/Switchboard.app/Contents/MacOS/sbctl top From a clone, swift build && .build/debug/sbctl. Command What it does sbctl top Live connections, busiest first sbctl dump The engine's whole model as JSON sbctl log query "process:Safari bytes>1MB" --since 7d Search the log sbctl log export Write the log as CSV or JSON lines sbctl geo 8.8.8.8 Where an address is and whose it is sbctl trust /Applications/Safari.app Who signed a program sbctl verify Check the engine against netstat and known traffic

title: How it works
heading: How it works
text: How it works Part Role SwitchboardCore The engine: connections, rates, names, the filter language. No system calls; fully testable SwitchboardSources Where data comes from: the system's network statistics, the kernel socket list, packet capture, process details switchboardd The optional root collector SwitchboardStore The log, on the SQLite that ships with macOS SwitchboardRender The graph, in Metal SwitchboardApp The window, in SwiftUI sbctl Diagnostics Some of the data comes from interfaces Apple does not document (the NetworkStatistics framework, the kernel socket list, PKTAP). Each is isolated, optional at run time, and reported on the Health tab, so a macOS update that breaks one costs

title: Releases
heading: Switchboard 0.1.1
text: 24 November 2026 · The release on GitHub A fix to the installer. Apart from its version number and the scripts below, the app is the same as 0.1.0.

title: Releases
heading: Fixed
text: The installer refused some Macs with "the download does not match the release's checksum", when the download was fine. It reported any failure of shasum as a mismatch. On a Mac with Intel-only programs left in /usr/local/bin by an old Homebrew, shasum cannot run at all without Rosetta, and Perl settings such as PERL5LIB can break macOS's own copy. The installer now uses only macOS's own tools. It says when the check could not run, and on a real mismatch shows what arrived instead. The scripts inside the app use only macOS's own tools too. These are the ones that install and remove the collector and download the location data, for anyone who runs them from a clone.

title: Releases
heading: Switchboard 0.1.0
text: 21 November 2026 · The release on GitHub The first release of Switchboard: a live picture of every network connection on your Mac, which program is talking, to whom, how much, and for how long. This is a beta. It is used daily on the author's Mac, but has only been run on macOS 27.

title: Releases
heading: What it does
text: Every connection, by program: process, user, remote address and port, bytes and rate each way, age, TCP state, round-trip time. Hostnames from the DNS answers and TLS handshakes it sees, once the collector is installed. Country, city, and network owner for each destination. Who signed each program, and which destinations are new. Six layouts (Constellation, Flow, Lanes, Globe, Hierarchy, Cyberspace) and six colour themes. A filter language, a timeline you can drag back, and a searchable log you can export. sbctl, a terminal viewer, at /Applications/Switchboard.app/Contents/MacOS/sbctl. It watches and never blocks or changes anything. It sends nothing anywhere. It uses the network itself only

title: Releases
heading: Known limits
text: Without the collector, macOS withholds about 5 to 8% of your own account's connections from Switchboard. It also reports other programs' new connections a few seconds late. The app uses 12 to 17% of a core in the Operator profile, over its 10% budget. It has run for hours at a stretch, not days. Memory with an hour of history is about 315 MB and still creeps up slowly. QUIC connections get names from DNS only. Encrypted DNS, ECH, and Private Relay all reduce what can be named.
